cultivar: Usually a lightly oxidised ball-rolled oolong from Si Ji Chun (Four Seasons), Jin Xuan or Qing Xin in Taiwan; Tieguanyin or other Fujian oolong in China
processing: A scented tea: finished ball-rolled oolong is layered with fresh osmanthus flowers so the leaf absorbs their aroma, then re-dried, often with some dried florets left in. Cheaper versions simply mix dried osmanthus into the tea or add a flavouring.
harvest_season: The base oolong comes from the spring or winter harvest; true scenting happens in the osmanthus bloom in late September and October, so the best lots are autumn-made.
appearance_dry: Tight green-brown oolong pellets flecked with tiny golden osmanthus florets.
appearance_wet: Unfurled green leaves with the little flowers floating among them.
taste_profile: Apricot, peach and honey from the osmanthus over a creamy, lightly floral oolong, with a sweet finish; the two aromas suit each other unusually well, so it reads as one tea rather than a tea plus a flavour.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or small pot, water around 90 °C, short steeps; boiling water pushes the florals into something cooked. Western style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes, two steeps. Lovely cold-brewed overnight.

vintage_note: Sold year-round on the current year's base oolong, with the aroma at its best within a year of scenting, so freshness matters more than any vintage. Traditionally scented lots are made in the autumn after the osmanthus bloom and may state the scenting season; most commercial packs do not. Visible florets are a good sign but not proof, since dried flowers can be added to a flavoured tea; an overwhelming candy-like smell on opening usually means flavouring.
description:
Osmanthus oolong is one of the happiest pairings in scented tea: the apricot-and-honey perfume of osmanthus flowers laid over a creamy, lightly oxidised oolong. Many of the versions seen in the West are Taiwanese, on a Four Seasons or Jin Xuan base from Nantou, and China makes its own on local oolongs.

The traditional method is the same as for jasmine tea: the finished leaf is mixed with freshly picked flowers in layers so it draws in the scent overnight, then separated and dried again, sometimes with a scattering of florets left in for looks. Osmanthus blooms for only a few weeks in autumn, so real scenting is seasonal; the rest of the year's production is either stored scented leaf or tea with dried flowers and flavouring added, which is a different and lesser thing.

In the cup it is peachy, honeyed and soft, with the oolong's cream and florals underneath and a sweetness that lasts; it is a tea that persuades people who think they dislike flavoured teas. Brew it gongfu-style with water around 90 °C and short steeps, or Western-style for three minutes, and keep the lid on. Boiling water flattens the fruit and brings out a cooked note.

It is sold on the current year's base tea and should be drunk within a year; look for a stated base (Jin Xuan, Four Seasons, Tieguanyin), for florets in the leaf, and for a scent that is pronounced but not sticky. Chinese versions are often sold as osmanthus Tieguanyin.

It pairs with almond pastries and mild cheese, and it is the natural next step after a plain Four Seasons oolong; for the flower alone, try a pinch of dried osmanthus in green tea.
history:
Osmanthus oolong is a scented tea, made by the same general idea as jasmine tea: finished leaf takes up the perfume of fresh flowers. Osmanthus scenting of tea is a Chinese practice, and the oolong version is made today in both Taiwan and China.

Little is documented about when or where this particular pairing began, and no maker or date can be credited with it. Treat any precise origin story on a packet with caution.
